The days lunedì–venerdì are stressed on the last syllable (written): lu-ne-DÌ, ve-ner-DÌ. Sabato is stressed on the first: SA-ba-to. Domenica on the second: do-ME-ni-ca.
"Mezza" and "mezzogiorno" are read with a long "dz": MED-dza, med-dzo-GIOR-no.
In "agli" (a + gli) and "figli", GLI = a soft "ly": A-lyi.
Venti, trenta, quaranta, cinquanta, sessanta, settanta, ottanta, novanta, cento. With 1 and 8, the vowel drops: ventuno, ventotto, trentuno.

FARE appears in many expressions where other languages use different verbs:
3. What time is it? Che ore sono?
For the time you use ESSERE in the plural ("sono le…"), except for one o'clock, midday and midnight:
sono le tre e un quarto
sono le quattro meno un quarto
"At what time?" = "A che ora?". The answer uses "alle" (a + le): "alle otto", "all'una", "a mezzogiorno".
In official timetables (trains, TV) the 24-hour clock is used: "Il treno parte alle diciotto e trenta."
Days are written in lower case and are masculine, except "domenica" (feminine). With the article they mean "every":
on Monday I'm going to the market
on Mondays I go to the market
Parts of the day: la mattina (in the morning), il pomeriggio (in the afternoon), la sera (in the evening), la notte (at night). "Stamattina" = this morning, "stasera" = this evening.
With "uno" and "otto", the tens drop their final vowel: vent-uno, vent-otto, trent-uno, quarant-otto. And "tre" at the end takes an accent: ventitré, trentatré.
